extracted.intended_audience: journalism scholars, media researchers, news editors, and journalism students
extracted.subtask_description: A concise set of newsworthiness criteria (the 10 news values) used to evaluate and select stories for newspapers, derived from Harcup & O'Neill's 2001 empirical update of Galtung & Ruge. Also notes key methodological critiques and limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: The power elite
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories concerning powerful individuals, organizations, or institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes coverage of people or entities with social, economic, or political power; such stories are treated as inherently newsworthy because of the actors' influence or status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Celebrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories concerning people who are already famous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes reporting on public figures whose fame attracts audience interest; differs from 'power elite' in that fame (entertainment/lifestyle prominence) rather than institutional power is the driver of newsworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entertainment
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories concerning sex, show-business, human interest, animals, an unfolding drama, or offering opportunities for humorous treatment, entertaining photographs, or witty headlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers soft-news topics that engage audiences through emotion, spectacle, visuals, or humour. Indicates that visual elements, opportunities for light treatment, and human-interest angles increase selection likelihood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories with an element of surprise and/or contrast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Events that violate expectations, contain contrasts, or present unexpected outcomes are more likely to be selected; surprise can be factual, situational, or tonal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bad news
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories with particularly negative overtones such as conflict or tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negative events (conflict, disaster, scandal) attract attention and are privileged in selection; 'bad news' is a core pull for audience interest and editorial prioritization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good news
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories with particularly positive overtones such as rescues and cures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive developments (successes, rescues, cures, uplifting outcomes) also constitute a clear category of newsworthiness, balancing the emphasis on negative events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories perceived as sufficiently significant either in the numbers of people involved or in potential impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scale matters: the larger the number affected or the greater the potential consequences, the more likely the story will be considered newsworthy; can be quantitative (casualties, economic impact) or qualitative (reach, precedent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories about issues, groups, and nations perceived to be relevant to the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audience-centred criterion: geographic, cultural, or topical proximity raises a story's salience; relevance is contingent on the target readership's interests and concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow-up
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories about subjects already in the news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuing coverage of an ongoing story increases newsworthiness; editors prioritise developments that extend or update previously reported items (seriality, persistence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspaper agenda
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that set or fit the newspaper's own agenda.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial priorities, campaign themes, or institutional angles shape selection: stories that align with or help construct a paper's agenda (political stance, campaign, advocacy) are favoured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key critiques and limitations of Galtung & Ruge (as noted by Harcup & O'Neill)
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical observations about the original Galtung & Ruge framework and its applicability to everyday news selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarizes methodological and substantive limitations identified by Harcup & O'Neill: (1) Galtung & Ruge studied only 'newsworthy' foreign events rather than the routine news flow, limiting generalizability; (2) original factors omitted entertainment, celebrity, and visual elements that Harcup & O'Neill found important; (3) some original factors (e.g., frequency, composition) describe news-production processes rather than inherent story attributes, complicating operationalization; (4) the notion of 'consonance' is difficult to operationalize empirically. Guidance: use the 10-value list as an updated, empirically grounded set of selection criteria but be aware of scope limits and the need to incorporate entertainment/visual/celebrity considerations and production-process influences when applying the framework.
